title: Market Day at Camp Two: the soft open
summary: The table goes up, the float is counted twice, the tally program runs live beside the cash, real customers pay real money, and whatever breaks goes in the bug diary because that is what a soft open is for.
materials: your inventory from the week 6 production run, counted before it leaves the house
the Market Day kit: cash box, coin float in change, price tags, sign board
your signs and price tags from week 7
the laptop with the tally program on it, charged, plus its charger
the micro:bit running the scrolling OPEN sign, with fresh batteries
a table and something to weigh the signs down if there is any wind
a paper tally sheet and a pen, as the backup for the backup
the Maker's Log and the bug diary

steps.title: Market Day
steps.body:
Three weeks ago this was a cost sheet. Today it is a table with your name behind it and people walking towards it who owe you nothing.

Today is a soft open, not a grand opening, and the difference matters. A soft open is the run where a shop finds out what breaks while the stakes are small: family, invited neighbours, one afternoon. Nobody is expecting it to be smooth. You are expecting it to be honest.

The design loop still runs the day, aimed at a new question. Ask: does the whole thing work when it is not just me looking at it? Imagine what could go wrong before it does: a customer who wants two and you only brought one, a coin you cannot make change for, a program that crashes with a queue in front of you, wind, rain, a small child who wants to help. Plan: the setup step below is the plan, and it happens before anyone arrives, not while they wait.

The day has three parts. Set up: table, signs, tags, float counted twice, tally program open and tested with a fake sale that you delete. Trade: serve people, type one line for every sale, make change by hand. Close: count the drawer, hold that count against what the program says, and announce out loud what happens next, which is the count and the loan.

One standing rule for the whole afternoon: every single thing that goes wrong goes in the bug diary, in the moment, in one line. Not the ones you found clever fixes for. All of them. The bug diary is the real product of a soft open, and a stand where nothing went wrong is a stand where nobody was watching.

Hand the device to a grown-up when you reach the next step. It is addressed to them and to your customers, not to you.

steps.title: For the family and the customers only
steps.body:
Family and neighbours, this step is addressed to you. Hand the device back after reading it.

The kindest thing you can do today is to be a real customer. That means paying the price on the tag without arguing it down and without rounding it up, and it means buying because you want the thing, not because you want them to feel good. A stand that sells out to sympathy teaches nothing and it will be the first thing they doubt afterwards.

So: buy what you actually want, and buy none if you want none. Walking away is allowed and it is useful. If you walk away, they learn more from one honest sentence about why than from a purchase, so tell them plainly: too dear, not for me, I already have one.

Pay awkwardly at least once between you, on purpose and without announcing it. Hand over a large note. Ask for two and see whether they can count that. Ask what it costs before you look at the tag. Change your mind at the last second. Every one of those is a real thing that happens at a real stand and every one of them is cheaper to meet today than on a busier day.

Ask them one question that is not about the product: how many did you make, what did one cost you, how did you land on that price. They have spent three weeks on those answers and they should get to use them standing up.

Two protections. The youngest customer goes first in the queue and gets to take their time counting their coins, however long that takes. And the money is theirs: the float and the takings are counted by them, and nobody helps unless they ask.

Five minutes on your typing site before the table goes out, while your hands are still calm. Warm up on the home row, then type the words the day is actually made of, ten times each, without looking down: sale, price, total, cash, profit, input, float, sold. The tally program wants steady fingers with a person standing in front of you, and this is the only chance to practise that today.

steps.title: Why one afternoon is a measurement, not a verdict
steps.body:
You will finish today with a number, and it is worth knowing in advance what that number can and cannot tell you.

Today's takings come from one street, one afternoon, one kind of weather, and whoever happened to be walking past. Scientists call that a sample, and the smaller a sample is, the more it wobbles. Run the identical stand next Saturday, change nothing at all, and the count comes out different. That difference is not you getting better or worse at anything. It is the wobble, and it is always there. That is exactly why the demand numbers you fed the pricing simulator in week 6 were guesses, and why big shops with real data still guess wrong.

So be careful with the sentence you say tonight. If four people buy, that is not proof the price is right. If nobody buys, that is not proof the price is wrong. One afternoon simply is not enough measuring to settle a question about how much the world wants a thing.

But here is what one afternoon settles completely. Does the tally program keep up when a person is standing in front of you? Does the float hold the coins you actually need for change? Do people understand what the thing is without being told twice? Can you make change while talking? Those are not wobbly questions. They are yes or no, and one queue answers every one of them for good.

That is the honest split, and it decides what you write down tonight. The total is a wobble. The breakages are facts. Which is why the bug diary matters more today than the takings do.

figure.alt: Market Day set up before the first customer: inventory counted onto the table, the float counted twice into the cash box, the tally program running on the laptop, the OPEN sign scrolling on the micro:bit, and a paper backup sheet ready underneath.

steps.title: Set up: everything before the first customer
steps.body:
Nothing here is allowed to happen while somebody is waiting. Do it all before the sign goes up.

The table: signs where they can be read from further away than you think, tags on or beside every single thing, and something heavy on anything that could blow away. Count your inventory onto the table and write the count down. You cannot know what sold if you never knew what arrived.

The float: count it once into the cash box, and then count it again a different way. The second count is not fussiness. It is the only thing standing between you and a closing number that lies to you tonight, because at close you subtract the float and any error in it walks straight into your profit. Write the float total down where you cannot lose it, and put it in the tally program too if the program asks for it.

The tally program: open a terminal in the folder the program lives in and start it the way you have started every program this season, by typing python, a space, and the file name, then pressing enter. On some machines the word is python3, and if that is yours, use python3 today too. Type in one pretend sale and check that the running cash and the running profit both change the way you expect. Then stop it the way you built it to stop, by typing done, the word it offers you beside the sale prompt, and start it again. The running totals live only inside the program while it is running, so starting it again is what clears the pretend sale, and there is no file to tidy up. If it ever freezes and will not take the word done, Ctrl and C held together stops it too. What you must not do is leave the pretend sale sitting inside the totals all afternoon, because every number the program shows you after that would be one sale wrong.

The OPEN sign: fresh batteries in the micro:bit, and watch the message scroll all the way round once before you trust it. That is your very first machine, working the door of your shop.

Last, the paper backup. A pen and a sheet with a line for every sale, sitting under the laptop. If the program dies mid-queue you do not debug in front of a customer; you write on paper, serve the person, and fix it after.
checklist: Inventory counted onto the table and the count written down before anything sold
The float counted twice, two different ways, and the total written down somewhere it cannot be lost
The tally program started, tested with one pretend sale, then stopped with done and started again, so the running totals began the day at zero
The OPEN sign scrolled all the way round once on fresh batteries
Paper tally sheet and pen sitting ready under the laptop as the backup

steps.title: Trade
steps.body:
Sign up. From here you are the shop.

The first customer is young and is going to be slow, and slow is fine. Let them count their coins into your hand themselves, out loud, all the way, without a single number said for them. That is the Sprout's job today and it is also the first sale of your life. Do not rush it because there is a queue. Tell the queue.

For every sale after that, the same rhythm every time: say the price out loud, take the money, count the change back into their hand out loud, then type the sale into the program before you look up at the next person. One line per sale, typed while it is still true. A sale you promise yourself you will type in a minute is a sale that will be wrong tonight.

Things will go wrong. That is the design of the day, not a fault in it. When something does, one line in the bug diary and carry on: the program threw an error and what the last line of it said, the float ran out of a coin, a tag fell off, two people arrived at once, you gave the wrong change and caught it, you gave the wrong change and they caught it. Write it while it stings; you will not remember it tonight and the sting is the useful part.

When someone asks a question you have an answer for, use the answer. How many did you make. What does one cost you. How did you pick that price. You have three weeks of work behind every one of those and standing behind a table is the only place that work becomes real.

And when someone walks away without buying, say thank you and mean it, then write down in one line what they said. A no with a reason attached is worth more than a yes you had to beg for.
checklist: The youngest customer went first and counted their own coins into my hand, with nobody counting for them
Every sale was typed into the program before I served the next person, or written on paper if the program was down
I counted the change back out loud on every sale
Every single thing that went wrong went into the bug diary in the moment, in one line, including the ones I fixed
Every no got a thank you and one written line saying why they walked away

steps.title: Close the stand
steps.body:
Sign down. Do the close properly while the table is still up, because a close done later at the kitchen counter is a close done from memory.

Count the cash box, all of it, out loud. Take away the float you wrote down at setup, and what is left is the money the afternoon actually brought in. Now count the inventory that came home and take it away from the count you wrote down at setup, and that is how many really sold.

Now hold the two stories side by side: what the cash box says, and what the tally program says. If they agree, say so out loud, because that is the program earning its keep. If they do not, do not fix the numbers to match. Write the gap down exactly as it is, and write one line about where you think it came from: a sale typed twice, a sale never typed, change given wrong, a price rung at the wrong number. A gap you write down honestly is a bug report. A gap you quietly close is a lie you will find again in week 9 when the ledger will not balance.

Save the day's work as a save point, and make the record real before you do. The tally program holds the day only while it is running: stop it and the sales are gone, because nothing it prints is ever written to a file. So before you close the terminal, make a new file beside the tally program, call it sales-day-one.txt, and put one line in it for every sale of the afternoon, in the same shape you typed them, reading them off the paper sheet and off the terminal you have not closed yet. Then git add the tally program and sales-day-one.txt, and git commit with a message that says what today was and what the gap was, if there was one. Leave it there. The venture code goes up on the internet in week 9, not today.

Then the closing announcement, out loud, to whoever is still standing there. Say two things. First, what happens next: the ledger closes next week, every cost gets counted, and the loan gets paid back in cash by hand before any profit is called profit. Second, one honest sentence about today: not the takings, but the thing that broke and what you are going to do about it.
checklist: Cash counted out loud, the float taken off, and the takings written down
Inventory that came home counted, so how many really sold is a count and not a guess
The cash box and the program compared, and any gap written down exactly as it is with one line on where it came from
Every sale written into sales-day-one.txt before the terminal was closed, then that file and the tally program committed as a save point, and nothing pushed anywhere
The closing announcement made out loud: the ledger and the loan next week, plus one honest sentence about what broke

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A photo of the table with the sign up and the tally program running beside the cash box, and a photo of the closing count with the two numbers side by side, the cash and what the program said. If a camera can stay rolling for one sale from start to finish, that is the one to keep: the price said out loud, the change counted back, and the line typed in. Add one sentence naming the worst thing that went wrong today and what you would change before you open again.

extras.title: Rewrite your best log
extras.body:
Your logs are the writing you do here, and writing gets better by rewriting, not by more of it. Pick your best log from this sprint and rewrite it once.

1. Read the log out loud. Mark every sentence that tries to say two things.
2. Rewrite so each sentence carries one idea. Split, do not shorten.
3. Find every adjective (hard, cool, weird) and replace it with a number or a fact: how many tries, how long, what broke.
4. Put the reason before the claim: "the loop ran twice, so the heart flashed twice" rather than "the heart flashed twice, because the loop ran twice".
5. Read both versions to someone and ask which one they could follow without you in the room.

What to notice: the rewrite is usually shorter and says more. That is the whole trick.
